label: Acf
description: The correlogram: autocorrelation at each lag as stems from zero, with the band inside which a lag is indistinguishable from noise. Two panels, because the pair is what a reader needs — the autocorrelation function says how far back the series remembers, the **partial** one how much of that memory is direct rather than inherited through the lags between. Lag 0 is dropped (it is 1 by definition and spends the whole vertical range saying so), the band is labelled with its formula and its n rather than left to be mistaken for a confidence interval on the coefficient, and the lags that cross it are coloured apart and listed — with the season named when the crossings are its multiples. description: Iso-lines over a scalar field z = f(x, y), with filled bands behind them. Use for a field that is measured or computed rather than estimated from points: a loss surface, a temperature, a potential, a model's output over two inputs. Every level is written on its own line — contour labels are an opt-in almost everywhere and almost nobody opts in, which leaves the reader a topography with no altitude — and the levels run on a geometric sequence by default, because a field spanning three orders of magnitude gets all its evenly spaced lines around the peaks and none in the basins. label: Control Chart
description: An individuals chart: one point per unit, a centre line, control limits, and four run rules applied and named when they fire. The usual version computes its limits from the standard deviation of every point, which is the error that empties the chart of meaning — a process that shifted has a large overall standard deviation *because* it shifted, so the limits widen until they swallow the shift they exist to catch. Limits here come from the mean moving range; `limit_from="sd"` draws the other version, and on the demo data that switch silences both sigma rules entirely. It also says, on the canvas, that these are control limits and not specification limits — the single most common confusion in the field — and draws spec limits apart, in another ink, when given.

Use for a small (2-6 category) part-of-whole breakdown: traffic by channel, budget by category, votes by candidate. **Count is not the only criterion: check the spread.** When the shares are close to each other, a donut is the worst choice available regardless of how few there are, because the eye compares neighbouring angles very poorly (Cleveland & McGill rank angle well below position and length). A real case that motivated this note: four segments at 27, 27, 24 and 22 percent rendered as a donut, where nothing could be ranked by looking and two wedges read identically. Sorted bars answer the same question instantly. Rule of thumb: if the largest share is less than about twice the smallest, use `bar` sorted descending, not `donut`.

label: Pareto
description: Bar chart sorted descending with a cumulative-percentage line. Use to identify the "vital few" factors that account for the majority of an effect (80/20 rule). **Two preconditions, both checkable before choosing it.** The data must be the WHOLE population, not a top-N already truncated upstream: run on a `LIMIT 10`, the cumulative line reaches 100% of those ten and any headline about "the total" is false, because the tail it was meant to expose was cut off before the chart saw it. label: Silhouette
description: One blade per sample, sorted inside its cluster, clusters stacked: the standard way to judge a clustering. The standard version reports one number — the overall mean — which is exactly the number that hides the problem, because three tight groups and one incoherent one average to "fine". Here the samples on the wrong side of zero (closer to another cluster than to their own) are counted per cluster and coloured apart, each cluster carries its own mean **and its own n**, and the overall mean is a rule across the figure. Below about two pixels a blade stops being a blade and the sorted profile is filled as one shape, which is the same information without the rasterising stripes.

label: Validation Curve
description: Score against one hyper-parameter, training and validation, with a band for the fold-to-fold range. Drawn to make one decision — which value to ship — and the usual version hands that decision back as a hump to eyeball. The peak is the wrong answer anyway: the argmax of a noisy validation curve overfits the validation set. This one performs the **one-standard-error rule** (take the simplest model within one standard error of the best), draws the threshold, marks both candidates, and says what the simpler model costs. `simpler_is` says which direction along the parameter is simpler, because only the caller knows.
